track.label: Technical Writing & Documentation
track.summary: Learn to write technical content professionals trust — from foundational clarity principles to API reference docs, user guides, SOPs, docs-as-code workflows, and documentation maintenance at scale.
track.name: tech-writing

phases.title: Writing Fundamentals for Technical Content
phases.description: Build the core habits of technical writing: clarity over cleverness, audience analysis, active voice, and document planning before you write a single word.

phases.title: API & Developer Documentation
phases.description: Write the documentation developers actually use — API reference, getting-started guides, code examples, and OpenAPI specs that reduce integration friction.

phases.title: User Guides & Help Content
phases.description: Create task-oriented documentation that helps real users accomplish goals — tutorials, how-to guides, FAQs, troubleshooting content, and UX microcopy.

phases.title: Process Documentation & SOPs
phases.description: Document how work gets done — standard operating procedures, runbooks, incident playbooks, and knowledge bases that keep teams aligned as they scale.

phases.title: Documentation Tools & Systems
phases.description: Work with the tools modern documentation teams use — Markdown, Git-based docs-as-code workflows, Confluence, Notion, and static site generators.

phases.title: Style, Review & Maintenance
phases.description: Manage documentation at scale: style guides, peer review processes, versioning, deprecation policies, and the ongoing work of keeping docs accurate and useful.

topics.title: Core Principles of Technical Writing
topics.description: Learn the foundational principles that distinguish technical writing from other forms: clarity, accuracy, conciseness, and accessibility — with practical exercises to apply each one.

steps.t: Apply clarity to a real document
steps.d: Take a paragraph from recent work documentation and rewrite each sentence to have one idea, active voice, and concrete nouns.
Review a technical document you've written and verify every technical term and spec against the actual source code or official docs.
Take a draft and cut 30% of words by removing redundancy, examples, and clarifications that a technical reader doesn't need.
Give your document to someone outside your specialization and ask them to explain back what they understood—if they miss the point, revise.
Based on these four principles, build a quick checklist you'll apply to your next three documents and mark which edits you make most often.

topics.title: Audience Analysis and User-Centered Writing
topics.description: Identify who you're writing for — their role, experience level, goals, and environment — and learn to adjust vocabulary, depth, and format accordingly.

steps.d: For a document you're about to write, answer: who's the main reader, what's their role, how much technical depth do they have, and what's their goal?
List five things your audience won't know about the system or process you're documenting that you take for granted.
Mark every technical term in your draft and decide which to explain in-line, link to a glossary, or assume the reader knows.
Find out how your audience will actually use your docs—quick reference, learning from scratch, or troubleshooting—then organize content around that need.
Share your draft with someone in your target audience and ask if the vocabulary level is right and if they'd find things in the order you've presented them.

topics.title: Structuring Technical Documents
topics.description: Plan and structure documents before writing — content outlines, progressive disclosure, chunking information, and using headings and lists effectively.

steps.d: For a document you need to write, create a three-level outline: main sections, subsections under each, and 2-3 points under each subsection.
Reorganize your outline so readers can get the quick answer first, then choose to dive deeper into details if they need them.
Ensure no section is longer than 2-3 pages and that each section teaches one concept or skill, with a clear heading that names what you'll learn.
Use headings, bullet points, and numbering to make structure visible—a reader should grasp your whole document by scanning headings.

steps.t: Test your structure on a reader
steps.d: Have someone unfamiliar with your topic use your table of contents to find what they'd expect to find, and note where they get lost.

topics.title: Writing API Reference Documentation
topics.description: Write the API reference documentation developers rely on — endpoint descriptions, parameter tables, request and response examples, error codes, and authentication guides.

steps.t: List all endpoints in your API
steps.d: Create a table of every endpoint you need to document with columns for HTTP method, path, and one-sentence description of what it does.
For each endpoint, write a description that names what it does, why a developer would use it, and what it returns (not how it works internally).
Build a template showing the exact request body, query parameters, and response for one endpoint with real, working examples.
For each endpoint, document the error codes it can return and write one sentence per error that explains what went wrong and what the developer should do.

steps.t: Verify your docs match the API
steps.d: Use your documentation to make a live API call exactly as written and confirm every part of the docs is accurate.

topics.title: Getting Started and Tutorial Writing
topics.description: Write the quick-start experience that gets developers to their first successful API call — a structured, reproducible tutorial with clear prerequisites, steps, and expected outcomes.

steps.d: Write down the exact steps a developer new to your API needs to take to make their first successful request: sign up, get credentials, make a call, see data.
List everything a developer needs before starting your tutorial: required credentials, libraries, tools, or accounts—nothing should be assumed.
Write 4-6 numbered steps that get a new developer from zero to their first working API call, with a code example they can copy for each step.
For each step, show the exact output or response the developer should see, so they know their implementation is working.
Have someone who's never used your API follow your tutorial without any help and note where they get stuck or confused.

topics.title: OpenAPI Specs and Spec-First Documentation
topics.description: Learn to read, write, and maintain OpenAPI (Swagger) specifications, and understand how spec-first development improves the consistency of API docs and SDKs.

steps.d: Find a live OpenAPI spec and read the paths, schemas, or security sections to see how an endpoint is formally defined.
Document one endpoint you work with as an OpenAPI spec, defining the path, method, parameters, and response schema in YAML or JSON.
Use a tool like Swagger UI or ReDoc to generate interactive documentation from your OpenAPI spec and compare it to your hand-written docs.
Compare your OpenAPI spec to your actual API implementation and note any differences in parameters, response fields, or required fields.

steps.t: Update your spec to match reality
steps.d: Fix your OpenAPI spec to accurately reflect the API as it works today, then regenerate documentation and verify it matches.

topics.title: Writing Effective User Guides and Tutorials
topics.description: Apply the Divio documentation system to distinguish between tutorials (learning-oriented) and how-to guides (task-oriented), and practise writing each type well.

steps.d: Review the Divio documentation system's distinction: tutorials teach, how-tos help you accomplish tasks, references explain, and explanations teach you why.
Review your recent documentation and label each piece as tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation, then note which types you're missing.
Create a tutorial that teaches a complete, isolated concept from start to finish (e.g., "How to set up your first deployment"), with a clear learning outcome.
Create a task-focused guide (e.g., "How to roll back a deployment") that assumes the reader knows the basics and just needs the steps.
Read both your tutorial and how-to and notice the differences: one teaches understanding, the other delivers speed—both are needed.

topics.title: FAQs, Troubleshooting, and Release Notes
topics.description: Write the support content users turn to when things go wrong — FAQs that actually answer questions, structured troubleshooting guides, and clear, user-facing release notes.

steps.d: List ten actual questions your support team gets or that you see in forums about your product.

steps.t: Build a FAQ with these questions
steps.d: Write a FAQ section answering your ten most common questions with brief, direct answers that solve the problem without extra context.
Write a troubleshooting guide organized by what the user is experiencing ("Feature X isn't working") rather than by error code, with diagnosis steps and fixes.
Write release notes for your next release explaining new features and fixes in language your users would use, with examples of what changed.
Give your FAQ or troubleshooting doc to someone with a real problem and see if they can solve it using only your docs.

topics.title: UX Writing and Microcopy
topics.description: Write the in-product text that guides users — button labels, error messages, empty states, and onboarding tooltips — applying UX writing principles to reduce friction.

steps.d: Take a screenshot of your application and list every piece of microcopy: button labels, error messages, empty state text, and confirmation prompts.
Take an error message that says "Error 403" and rewrite it to explain what went wrong and what the user should do: "Access denied. Only admins can delete users."
Find an empty state in your product (inbox with no messages, list with no items) and write text that explains what should be there and how to get started.
Identify a button, field, or option in your product with unclear labeling and test it with a user—if they hesitate, rewrite it.
Implement three of your rewritten messages in your product and measure if support questions about those features go down.

topics.title: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
topics.description: Write SOPs that teams actually follow — clear scope, numbered steps, decision points, roles and responsibilities, and the right level of detail for your audience.

steps.d: Choose a process your team follows and list every step from start to finish, including all decision points and edge cases.
Transform your process map into a numbered SOP with clear steps, including what to do if something goes wrong.
Add a section to your SOP naming who does each major step and what decisions they own.
Mark which steps are non-negotiable and which have flexibility, so team members know where they need to improvise vs. follow exactly.

steps.t: Train someone new with your SOP
steps.d: Have a new team member follow your SOP to complete the process with zero background knowledge and note where your instructions fail.

topics.title: Runbooks and Incident Documentation
topics.description: Create operational runbooks and incident playbooks that help engineering teams respond quickly under pressure — structured, scannable, and tested before they're needed.

steps.d: Pick a real incident or outage your team has responded to and outline the diagnosis steps the on-call engineer followed.
Create a step-by-step incident playbook: what to check first, what to check if that's normal, escalation paths, and rollback procedures.
Document what symptoms indicate this incident, how to measure its impact on users, and what the recovery state looks like.
Give your incident runbook to someone unfamiliar with the system and ask them to follow it to isolate a simulated problem.
After your team handles a real incident, review your playbook and update it with anything you missed or got wrong.

topics.title: Knowledge Base Architecture
topics.description: Design a knowledge base that scales — taxonomy, search-optimised naming, content types, and the organisational model that helps users find what they need without asking.

steps.t: List all documentation types you have
steps.d: Catalog every piece of documentation your team produces: guides, FAQs, how-tos, policies, references, training materials.
Group these documents into a logical hierarchy: what's top-level, what's second-level, and how should someone find what they need?

steps.t: Name documents by what they do
steps.d: Review your navigation and document titles—change names from "System Overview" to "How to deploy for the first time" if that's what the doc is for.
Review your most-needed documents and add keywords to their titles and first sentences so someone searching for common terms finds them.

steps.t: Map the user journey through docs
steps.d: Trace how a new user would find the information they need from first question to final task—note dead ends and add missing links.

topics.title: Docs-as-Code with Markdown and Git
topics.description: Treat documentation like software — use Markdown, Git version control, pull requests, and CI pipelines to manage docs alongside code with the same quality standards.

steps.d: Create a Git repository for your documentation with Markdown files in a clear folder structure that mirrors your documentation hierarchy.
Configure your repository to run a check on pull requests—at minimum, a linter or spell-check so docs quality improves before merge.
Write a CONTRIBUTING.md file explaining how to fork, edit, and submit a pull request for documentation changes.
Set up a static site generator (Jekyll, Hugo, or MkDocs) that builds your documentation into a published site automatically on each commit.
Deploy your generated documentation to a public URL with CI/CD so every merged PR automatically publishes.

topics.title: Confluence and Notion for Team Documentation
topics.description: Use Confluence and Notion effectively for internal documentation — page hierarchies, templates, databases, and practices that prevent content from going stale.

steps.d: List all spaces, pages, and databases in your Confluence or Notion workspace and identify duplicates, outdated content, or poorly organized sections.
Build a page template in Confluence or Notion that your team will use for all new documentation—define heading structure, sections, and required fields.
Define how pages will be named so they're sortable and findable: date first for project logs, category first for processes.

steps.t: Set up a database for tracking
steps.d: In Notion or Confluence, create a database or macro that tracks documentation type, owner, last updated date, and status (current, draft, outdated).
Pick one Confluence space or Notion database and reorganize it following your template and naming rules, then measure findability improvement.

topics.title: Static Site Generators for Documentation
topics.description: Set up and customise developer documentation sites using Docusaurus or MkDocs — the standard open-source tools for publishing beautiful, searchable documentation portals.

steps.d: Download and run Docusaurus or MkDocs on your machine and confirm you can build and preview the example site.
Build the folder structure and initial pages for your documentation site: home, guides, API reference, FAQ.
Edit the docusaurus.config.js or mkdocs.yml to set your site name, logo, color scheme, and navigation structure.
Write or convert three existing documents into your site's Markdown format and build the site locally to see it rendered.
Push your site to GitHub Pages, Netlify, or another free hosting and get your documentation live on the web.

topics.title: Style Guides and Terminology Management
topics.description: Create or adopt a style guide that enforces consistency — voice and tone, formatting rules, spelling decisions, and a product-specific terminology glossary.

steps.t: Adopt or create a style guide
steps.d: Choose a public style guide (Google, Microsoft, or Shopify) or create your own, documenting your decisions on terminology, voice, and grammar.
List 20-30 terms your product uses and define each one consistently—use this glossary to link from your documentation.
Write examples showing how your documentation should sound: formal vs. casual, second person vs. third, and common phrases to use or avoid.
Define rules for headings, code blocks, lists, and links so your docs look consistent across all writers and platforms.

steps.t: Create a quick reference for writers
steps.d: Build a one-page checklist or template that any writer can use to ensure they follow your style guide before submitting.

topics.title: Peer Review and Editing Processes
topics.description: Build a lightweight review workflow for documentation — what to review for, how to give feedback that improves clarity without rewriting the author's voice.

steps.d: Document the peer review process: who reviews what, what they look for, timelines for feedback, and how to handle disagreements.
Build a checklist for reviewers covering: accuracy, clarity, completeness, style compliance, and whether examples work as written.
Apply your review checklist to a draft document and leave detailed feedback on accuracy, clarity, examples, and style issues.
Take feedback from your review and implement changes, noting which suggestions improved the document most.
Create a standard review comment template your team will use in pull requests or shared docs to give consistent, actionable feedback.

topics.title: Documentation Maintenance and Versioning
topics.description: Keep documentation accurate over time — audit processes, deprecation strategies, versioned docs for multiple product releases, and sunsetting outdated content gracefully.

steps.d: Review your oldest documentation and identify what's likely outdated: feature names, screenshots, workflow steps, or tool references.
Follow the steps in three older documents and verify they still work—note what's broken and what's just phrased in old language.
For products with multiple releases, set up a versioning structure so docs for v1.0, v2.0, etc. are available side-by-side.
For outdated features or workflows, add deprecation banners to docs and create a redirect to the new approach.
When documentation changes significantly, update a changelog noting what changed, when, and where to find the old version if needed.
